segments.line: Four days later, you've been perfect. No stunts. No falls.
Bar full.
Then you hear Ellie.
She's standing on top of the old tree house in the backyard.
Not inside it. On the roof.
'Look! ' she shouts. 'I've got the bar too! Watch me! '
She doesn't. There's nothing over her head. Just air. The bar only works for you.
And then the roof board cracks.
That roof is about ten feet up.
A fall from there hits the ground at around seventeen miles an hour.
In a game, that's nothing.
For a seven- year- old, it's a trip to the emergency room.
And a fall from that roof takes less than one second. That's all the time there is.
You run. And this time, you use real physics, not game physics.
What hurts in a fall isn't the speed. It's stopping too fast.
Stop over a longer distance, and the force drops. Make the stop ten times longer, and it's ten times gentler.
That's exactly how an airbag works.
It's why stunt people fall onto big soft air cushions, and why gymnasts land on thick mats. Soft and deep beats strong arms, every time.
So you don't try to catch her with your arms. You grab the giant beanbag off the porch,
throw it under the tree house, and
dive in underneath it.
Ellie lands on the beanbag, and the beanbag lands on you.
She's safe. She's laughing, even.
You're not laughing. Your bar was full. Now it's flashing red.
Zero.
